items.title: Focus Question: How is pitch controlled in a guitar and in a trombone?

answer.html: By changing the frequency of the vibrating part. A guitarist shortens the vibrating length of a string with a finger on a fret (or changes its tension when tuning). A trombonist slides the tube in or out to change the length of the vibrating air column. Resonance then reinforces that frequency.

items.title: Get It? (page 370): How does a guitarist play higher pitched notes?

answer.html: The player presses the string against a fret, which shortens the vibrating length of the string. A shorter string vibrates faster (higher frequency), so the pitch is higher. Tightening a string does the same thing.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts, Cause and Effect (page 370): A 512 Hz tuning fork is held over a tube that is closed at the bottom by water. Moving the tube up and down changes the loudness. Develop a mathematical representation and find the first three loud positions.

body.html: Fork frequency 𝑓= 512 Hz, air at 20°C so 𝑣= 343 m/s. The air column has length 𝐿 (closed at the water end, open at the top). Find the lengths that give loud sounds.
The water surface is a closed end (displacement node) and the open top is an antinode. A standing wave fits only if 𝐿 is an odd number of quarter wavelengths.
First compute 𝑣/ (4𝑓):
The spacing between loud positions is 𝛥𝐿= 𝜆/ 2 = 𝑣/ (2𝑓) = 0.335 m, matching 0.502 −0.167.

answer.html: 𝐿= (2𝑛−1)<sub> </sub><sup>𝑣</sup> <sub>4</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>; the sound is loudest at 𝐿≈16.7 cm, 50.2 cm, 83.7 cm (spaced by 33.5 cm) and softer in between.

check.html: At 𝐿<sub>1</sub> the wavelength is 𝜆= 4𝐿<sub>1</sub> = 0.670 m and 𝑓= 343 / 0.670 = 512 Hz.

items.title: Figure 12 (Identify): A pipe closed at one end and open at the other has length 0.60 m and resonates with its third harmonic (𝐿= 3𝜆/ 4). Where are the pressure nodes (mean pressure) and pressure antinodes (largest pressure swings)?

body.html: 𝐿= 0.60 m, 𝐿= 3𝜆/ 4. Find 𝜆 and the positions measured from the closed end.

Pressure nodes are where the pressure stays at its average value; they are at the open end (air there stays at atmospheric pressure). Pressure antinodes are at the closed end and halfway between nodes. Adjacent pressure nodes are 𝜆/ 2 apart.
The open end (0.60 m) is a pressure node; the next node is 𝜆/ 2 = 0.40 m closer, at 0.20 m. The antinodes are at the closed end (0 m) and at 0.40 m, midway between the two nodes.

answer.html: Pressure nodes at 0.20 m and 0.60 m (the open end) from the closed end; pressure antinodes at 0 m (the closed end) and 0.40 m.

check.html: Nodes and antinodes alternate every 𝜆/ 4 = 0.20 m: 0, 0.20, 0.40, 0.60 m.

items.title: Get It? (page 372): Adjacent displacement nodes in an open pipe are 0.35 m apart. Explain the difference between a node and an antinode and find the wavelength.

body.html: Distance between adjacent nodes = 0.35 m. Find 𝜆 and the distance from a node to the nearest antinode.
A node is a point of zero displacement; an antinode is a point of maximum displacement. Adjacent nodes are 𝜆/ 2 apart, and a node and the nearest antinode are 𝜆/ 4 apart.

answer.html: Air particles do not move at a displacement node but move the most at an antinode. 𝜆= 0.70 m, and a node and its nearest antinode are 0.175 m apart.

check.html: Two node-to-antinode spacings (2 × 0.175) equal the 0.35 m node-to-node spacing.

items.title: Figure 14 (Explain): A 0.85 m pipe is played once with both ends open and once with one end closed. Compare the fundamental wavelengths and frequencies.

body.html: 𝐿= 0.85 m, 𝑣= 343 m/s. Find 𝜆 and 𝑓<sub>1</sub> for each case.
An open pipe has an antinode at both ends, so 𝐿= 𝜆/ 2. A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so 𝐿= 𝜆/ 4.
closed: 𝜆= 4𝐿= 3.40 m,

answer.html: The open pipe resonates when its length is a whole number of half wavelengths ( 𝜆= 1.70 m, 𝑓<sub>1</sub> ≈202 Hz). The closed pipe resonates at odd multiples of a quarter wavelength ( 𝜆= 3.40 m, 𝑓<sub>1</sub> ≈101 Hz), so the same-length closed pipe sounds an octave lower.

check.html: The closed pipe's wavelength is twice as long, so its frequency is half as large (101 Hz versus 202 Hz).

items.title: Get It? (page 373): Predict whether a 0.375 m pipe that resonates with a tuning fork of wavelength 0.50 m is open or closed.

body.html: Compare 𝐿 with multiples of 𝜆/ 2 (open pipe) and odd multiples of 𝜆/ 4 (closed pipe).
𝜆/ 2 = 0.25 m, and 0.375 m is 1.5 of these, not a whole number, so an open pipe is ruled out. 𝜆/ 4 = 0.125 m, and 0.375 m = 3 (0.125 m) = 3𝜆/ 4, which is an odd multiple of 𝜆/ 4.

answer.html: The pipe is closed, because 𝐿= 3𝜆/ 4.

check.html: An open pipe would need 0.25 m or 0.50 m, neither of which is 0.375 m.

items.title: Get It? (page 374): Relationship between string tension and wave speed

body.html: A guitar string's tension is increased to four times its original value with the length and mass unchanged. By what factor does the wave speed (and the fundamental frequency) change?
𝑣= √𝐹<sup>T</sup> / 𝜇, and 𝑓<sup>1</sup> = 𝑣/ (2𝐿).

answer.html: The wave speed doubles, and since 𝑓<sub>1</sub> = 𝑣/ (2𝐿) with 𝐿 fixed, the fundamental frequency doubles (one octave higher).

check.html: Speed grows only as the square root of the tension, so a factor of 4 in tension gives a factor of 2 in speed.

check.html: Slower than the 343 m/s in air, as expected for a gas of heavier molecules.

items.title: 14 (Lesson 2, Practice Problem 2): Unknown tuning fork frequency

body.html: Resonances of an unknown fork in a tube occur at spacing 31.8 cm = 0.318 m on a cool day when the air is at 15°C. Find 𝑓.
First find the speed at 15°C from 𝑣= 343 m/s + (0.6 m/s / °C) 𝛥𝑇. Spacing = 𝜆/ 2, and 𝑓= 𝑣/ 𝜆.

answer.html: 𝑓≈535 Hz

check.html: Plausible audible tuning fork frequency (near the note C5).

items.title: 15 (Lesson 2, Practice Problem 3): Resonance spacing for a 587 Hz fork at 10°C

body.html: 𝑓= 587 Hz, air at 10°C. Find the spacing 𝛥𝐿.

body.html: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental of 130 Hz. Find its next two resonances and describe how they relate to the fundamental.
A closed pipe resonates only at odd multiples of the fundamental: 𝑓<sub>𝑛</sub>= 𝑛𝑓<sub>1</sub> with 𝑛= 1, 3, 5, …

answer.html: The fundamental is the lowest resonance (130 Hz). The next two harmonics are 390 Hz and 650 Hz, whole-number (odd) multiples of the fundamental; the even multiples (260 Hz, 520 Hz) are missing for a closed pipe.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 2) Problem 17: Name the vibrating object that produces the sound of (a) a flute, (b) a trombone, (c) a kettle drum, (d) a piano.

answer.html: (a) flute: the air stream splitting on the edge of the mouth hole, which sets the air column vibrating; (b) trombone: the player's lips (and the air column); (c) kettle drum: the stretched drumhead (membrane); (d) piano: the struck strings, whose vibrations are passed to the sounding board.

items.title: 18: Why is the lowest pipe of a pipe organ much longer than the highest pipe?

body.html: For a pipe, 𝑓<sub>1</sub> ∝1 / 𝐿 (for example 𝑓<sub>1</sub> = 𝑣/ (4𝐿) for a closed pipe), so a lower fundamental needs a longer air column.

answer.html: The lowest note has the lowest frequency and so the longest wavelength. Resonance needs a column about a quarter (or half) wavelength long (𝐿∝𝜆), so the lowest pipe must be much longer than the highest.

items.title: 19: What is the length of a closed tube, relative to the wavelength, for its strongest (fundamental) resonance?

answer.html: The length must be a quarter wavelength, 𝐿= 𝜆/ 4 (the fundamental, which gives the strongest resonance). Odd multiples of 𝜆/ 4 (3𝜆/ 4, 5𝜆/ 4, … ) also resonate.

items.title: 20: Find the next three harmonics of a 294 Hz guitar note.

body.html: A string's harmonics are whole-number multiples of the fundamental: 𝑓<sub>𝑛</sub>= 𝑛𝑓<sub>1</sub> with 𝑓<sub>1</sub> = 294 Hz.

answer.html: 588 Hz, 882 Hz, and 1176 Hz (the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th harmonics).

check.html: Each is an integer multiple of 294 Hz.

items.title: 21(a): Frequency of a closed organ pipe of length 1.85 m

body.html: Closed pipe, 𝐿= 1.85 m, 𝑣= 343 m/s.
Closed pipe fundamental: 𝑓<sub>1</sub> = 𝑣/ (4𝐿).

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>1</sub> ≈46.4 Hz

check.html: A long pipe gives a very low note, as expected.

items.title: 21(b): A second pipe produces a 0.90 Hz beat with the first; how much too long is it?

body.html: 𝑓<sub>beat</sub> = 0.90 Hz, 𝑓<sub>1</sub> = 46.35 Hz. A pipe that is too long has too low a frequency, so 𝑓<sub>2</sub> = 𝑓<sub>1</sub> −0.90 Hz. Find 𝐿<sub>2</sub> −𝐿<sub>1</sub>.
𝑓<sub>beat</sub> = | 𝑓<sub>A</sub> −𝑓<sub>B</sub>|; then 𝐿= 𝑣/ (4𝑓).

answer.html: The second pipe is too long by about 0.037 m (about 3.7 cm).

check.html: Lengthening a pipe lowers its frequency, so a longer pipe gives the lower frequency we used.

items.title: 22: A flute, a clarinet, and a tuning fork all sound the note A at 440 Hz. Why do they sound different?

answer.html: The tuning fork produces almost only the fundamental (a nearly pure sine wave), while the flute and clarinet each produce the fundamental plus their own mix of harmonics with different relative amplitudes. This difference in the sound spectrum changes the waveform shape even though the fundamental frequency is the same, and it is called timbre, or tone quality.

items.title: 23: Beats between a tuning fork and a 440 Hz tuning fork

body.html: An unknown fork A and a 440 Hz fork B beat at 4 Hz. When a small piece of tape is stuck on fork A (which lowers its frequency slightly), the beat rate rises to 6 Hz. Find 𝑓<sub>A</sub>.
𝑓<sub>beat</sub> = | 𝑓<sub>A</sub> −𝑓<sub>B</sub>| gives two possibilities, 444 Hz or 436 Hz. Adding mass lowers the frequency, which tells us which one is right.

If 𝑓<sub>A</sub> = 444 Hz, lowering it moves it toward 440 Hz and the beat rate would drop below 4 Hz. If 𝑓<sub>A</sub> = 436 Hz, lowering it moves it farther from 440 Hz and the beat rate would rise, as observed.

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>A</sub> = 436 Hz. (Without the tape clue, the beats alone allow 436 Hz or 444 Hz.)

check.html: With the tape the fork is a bit lower, for example 434 Hz, giving a 6 Hz beat against 440 Hz.

items.title: 24 (Critical Thinking): Pressing a struck tuning fork's handle against a guitar body, a wall, and a cardboard box

answer.html: The sound becomes much louder when the handle touches an object. A fork alone moves very little air, but the object's large surface is forced to vibrate at the fork's frequency and pushes much more air, as a sounding board does. The pitch is the same, but the fork's vibration dies out sooner because its energy is transferred to the air faster. Different objects give somewhat different loudness and tone because of their size and material (the guitar body, which is designed to resonate, would be especially effective).

items.title: 3D Thinking: STEM at Work (page 380): Research a technology that uses echolocation and summarize how it works.

body.html: No data are given; this is a short research and writing task. Here is a model response.

Echo ranging: distance 𝑑= 𝑣𝑡/ 2, where 𝑡 is the round-trip time. Work (sample paragraph): A fishing-boat depth sounder sends a short pulse of ultrasound (about 200 kHz) straight down into the sea. The pulse reflects from the sea floor and returns to the transducer. The electronics measure the round-trip time 𝑡 and compute the depth 𝑑= 𝑣𝑡/ 2, using 𝑣≈1535 m/s in seawater. For example, an echo returning after 0.320 s means 𝑑= (1535)(0.320) / 2 ≈246 m. A stronger echo from a school of fish appears as a mark above the bottom.

answer.html: Sample answer: A depth sounder (like bat echolocation and ship sonar) times an echo and computes distance 𝑑= 𝑣𝑡/ 2. Any other echolocation technology (parking sensors, medical ultrasound, self-driving car sensors) with a clear explanation of the emit, reflect, detect, and calculate steps is acceptable.

check.html: The round trip covers 2 × 246 = 492 m in 0.320 s, which is 1538 m/s, the speed of sound in seawater.

items.title: 1: Claim: Should you try your experiment?

answer.html: No. The experiment as designed is not practical or safe with a car.

items.title: 2: Evidence and Reasoning

answer.html: Evidence: a minor third (470 Hz versus 392 Hz) requires a source speed of 𝑣<sub>s</sub> ≈57.2 m/s (about 206 km/h, or 128 mph). Reasoning: that speed is far above legal limits and unsafe for a car carrying a clarinet player (and wind and engine noise would make the pitch hard to judge). A smaller interval needs a lower speed: a half step (ratio 15: 16) needs 𝑣<sub>s</sub> = (343)(1 −15 / 16) = 21.4 m/s (about 48 mph). The team could use that smaller interval, or a recording, a speaker on a safer platform, or an electronic frequency analyzer. So the claim is to modify the experiment to use a smaller interval and a measurement, not to attempt a minor third in a car.

check.html: 57.2 / 343 = 0.167, equal to 1 −5 / 6, as the formula requires.

items.title: Focus Question: How is pitch controlled in a musical instrument?

answer.html: By changing the frequency of the vibrating part. Air-column instruments change the length of the vibrating air column; strings change their length, tension (or thickness); vocal cords change their muscular tension. Resonance then reinforces that frequency.

items.title: Get It? (page 370): How does a vocalist sing higher pitched notes?

answer.html: The singer increases the muscular tension on the vocal cords, so they vibrate faster (higher frequency) and produce a higher pitch.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts, Cause and Effect (page 370): Moving the tube in Figure 10 changes the loudness. Develop a mathematical representation.

body.html: Fork frequency 𝑓, speed of sound 𝑣, air column length 𝐿 (closed at the water end, open at the top). Relate them to explain the loud and soft sounds.
The water surface is a closed end (displacement node) and the open top is an antinode. A standing wave fits only if 𝐿 is an odd number of quarter wavelengths.
Using 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓:

Resonant lengths are 𝜆/ 4, 3𝜆/ 4, 5𝜆/ 4, … , spaced by 𝛥𝐿= 𝜆/ 2 = 𝑣/ (2𝑓). When the tube is moved so that 𝐿 equals one of these values, the reflected waves reinforce the fork's waves (resonance) and the sound is loud. For other lengths the waves do not reinforce each other, so the sound is soft.

answer.html: 𝐿= (2𝑛−1)<sub> </sub><sup>𝜆</sup>
<sub>4</sub><sub>𝑓</sub>; sound is loudest at these lengths (spaced by 𝜆/ 2) and softer in between.

check.html: For 𝑓= 392 Hz, 𝑣= 343 m/s: 𝑣/ (4𝑓) = 0.219 m, close to the 21.0 cm first resonance in Example Problem 2 (the small difference is the end correction).

items.title: Figure 12 (Identify): Which are the areas of mean atmospheric pressure in the air pressure graphs?

body.html: In the pressure graphs of Figure 12, the labels show "pressure node (average-pressure region)" and "pressure antinode (high- or low-pressure region)."

answer.html: The pressure nodes: the closed pipe has one at its open top, and the open pipe has them at both open ends. (In the figure the nodes of the pressure curve are where the pressure stays at average value, and the antinodes are where it swings between high and low.)

items.title: Get It? (page 372): Explain the difference between a node and an antinode on a displacement graph.

answer.html: A displacement node is a point where the air particles do not move (zero displacement), such as at a closed end. A displacement antinode is a point of maximum displacement, such as at an open end. Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are 𝜆/ 2 apart.

items.title: Figure 14 (Explain): How does the length at which an open pipe resonates differ from that of a closed pipe?

answer.html: A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so it resonates when 𝐿= 𝜆/ 4, 3𝜆/ 4, 5𝜆/ 4, … (odd multiples of a quarter wavelength). An open pipe has an antinode at both ends, so it resonates when 𝐿= 𝜆/ 2, 𝜆, 3𝜆/ 2, … (even multiples of a quarter wavelength, i.e., whole numbers of half wavelengths). For the same length, the open pipe's fundamental wavelength is half as long, so its frequency is twice as high.

items.title: Get It? (page 373): Predict whether a 0.39 m pipe that resonates with a tuning fork of wavelength 0.78 m is open or closed.

body.html: Compare 𝐿 to 𝜆 for each pipe type.
𝜆/ 2 = 0.39 m, which equals 𝐿. An open pipe resonates at 𝐿= 𝜆/ 2. A closed pipe would need 𝐿= 𝜆/ 4 = 0.195 m, 3𝜆/ 4 = 0.585 m, and so on, and none of these equals 0.39 m.

answer.html: The pipe is open, because 𝐿= 𝜆/ 2.

check.html: 0.39 m is not an odd multiple of 0.195 m, so a closed pipe is ruled out.

items.title: Get It? (page 374): Relationship between string tension and wave speed

answer.html: The greater the tension, the greater the wave speed on the string (𝑣= √𝐹<sup>T</sup> / 𝜇, so speed grows with the square root of the tension). Higher speed means higher standing-wave frequencies, which is how strings are tuned.

answer.html: (a) human voice: the vocal cords; (b) clarinet: the vibrating reed (and the air column it drives); (c) tuba: the player's lips (and the air column); (d) violin: the strings, whose vibrations are passed to the sounding board.

items.title: 18: Why is the tuba's tube much longer than a cornet's?

body.html: For a closed-pipe-type air column, 𝑓<sub>1</sub> = 𝑣/ (4𝐿), so a longer column has a lower fundamental.

answer.html: The tuba plays much lower notes. Low frequencies have long wavelengths, and resonance requires a long air column (𝐿∝𝜆), so the tuba's tube must be longer.

items.title: 19: Length of an open tube relative to the wavelength for strongest resonance

answer.html: The length must be half a wavelength, 𝐿= 𝜆/ 2 (the fundamental, which gives the strongest resonance). Whole-number multiples of 𝜆/ 2 also resonate.

items.title: 20: Next three harmonics of a 370 Hz violin note

body.html: A string's harmonics are whole-number multiples of the fundamental: 𝑓<sub>𝑛</sub>= 𝑛𝑓<sub>1</sub> with 𝑓<sub>1</sub> = 370 Hz.

answer.html: 740 Hz, 1110 Hz, and 1480 Hz (the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th harmonics).

check.html: Each is an integer multiple of 370 Hz.

items.title: 21(a): Frequency of a closed organ pipe of length 2.40 m

body.html: Closed pipe, 𝐿= 2.40 m, 𝑣= 343 m/s.
Closed pipe fundamental: 𝑓<sub>1</sub> = 𝑣/ (4𝐿).

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>1</sub> ≈35.7 Hz

check.html: A long pipe gives a very low note, as expected.

items.title: 21(b): Second pipe producing a 1.40 Hz beat; how much too long?

body.html: 𝑓<sub>beat</sub> = 1.40 Hz, 𝑓<sub>1</sub> = 35.73 Hz. A pipe that is too long has too low a frequency, so 𝑓<sub>2</sub> = 𝑓<sub>1</sub> −1.40 Hz. Find 𝐿<sub>2</sub> −𝐿<sub>1</sub>.
𝑓<sub>beat</sub> = | 𝑓<sub>A</sub> −𝑓<sub>B</sub>|; then 𝐿= 𝑣/ (4𝑓).

answer.html: The second pipe is too long by about 0.098 m (about 9.8 cm).

check.html: Lengthening a pipe lowers its frequency, so a longer pipe gives the lower frequency we used.

items.title: 22: Why do different instruments sound different when they play the same note?

answer.html: Each instrument produces its own mix of harmonics with different relative amplitudes (its sound spectrum), giving a different waveform shape even at the same fundamental frequency. This difference is called timbre, or tone quality.

items.title: 23: Beats between a tuning fork and a 392 Hz tuning fork

body.html: 𝑓<sub>beat</sub> = 3 Hz, 𝑓<sub>B</sub> = 392 Hz. Find 𝑓<sub>A</sub>.
𝑓<sub>beat</sub> = | 𝑓<sub>A</sub> −𝑓<sub>B</sub>| gives two possibilities.
𝑓<sub>A</sub> = 392 Hz ± 3 Hz.

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>A</sub> = 395 Hz or 389 Hz. (The beat alone cannot tell which; adding a bit of mass to one fork would settle it.)

items.title: 24 (Critical Thinking): Pressing a struck tuning fork's handle against a desk, door, and filing cabinet

answer.html: The sound becomes much louder when the handle touches an object. A fork alone moves very little air, but the object's large surface is forced to vibrate at the fork's frequency and pushes much more air, as a sounding board does. The pitch is the same, but the fork's vibration dies out faster because its energy is being transferred to the air more quickly. Different objects give somewhat different loudness and tone because of their size and material.

items.title: 3D Thinking: STEM at Work (page 380): Research a technology that uses echolocation and summarize how it works.

body.html: No data are given; this is a short research and writing task. Here is a model response.

Echo ranging: distance 𝑑= 𝑣𝑡/ 2, where 𝑡 is the round-trip time. Work (sample paragraph): An ultrasonic parking sensor in a car bumper sends out short pulses of sound at a frequency far above human hearing (about 40 kHz). The pulse reflects off an obstacle and returns to the sensor. The electronics measure the round-trip time 𝑡 and compute the distance 𝑑= 𝑣𝑡/ 2, using 𝑣≈343 m/s in air. For example, an echo returning after 5.8 ms means 𝑑= (343)(0.0058) / 2 ≈1.0 m. As the distance shrinks, the car beeps faster to warn the driver.

answer.html: Sample answer: Ultrasonic parking sensors (like bat echolocation and ship sonar) time an echo and compute distance 𝑑= 𝑣𝑡/ 2. Any other echolocation technology (sonar, medical ultrasound, self-driving car sensors) with a clear explanation of the emit, reflect, detect, and calculate steps is acceptable.

check.html: An echo of 5.8 ms gives about 1 m, a sensible parking distance.

items.title: 1: Claim: Should you try your experiment?

answer.html: No. The experiment as designed is not practical or safe with a car.

items.title: 2: Evidence and Reasoning

answer.html: Evidence: a major third (550 Hz versus 440 Hz) requires a source speed of 𝑣<sub>s</sub> ≈68.6 m/s (about 247 km/h, or 153 mph). Reasoning: that speed is far above legal speed limits and unsafe for a car, with a musician playing a trumpet inside it (and wind and engine noise would make the pitch hard to judge). A smaller interval would need a lower speed, for example a half step (ratio 277/262) at about 18.6 m/s as in Practice Problem 5, or the team could use a recording or a speaker mounted on a safer platform, or an electronic frequency analyzer. So the claim is to modify the experiment to use a smaller interval and a measurement, not to attempt a major third in a car.
